title: [round · research-lab shape] Design the experiment that would falsify this paper
body:
> **Simulated interview round.** The shape a research-lab or applied-science panel runs, with the
> rubric attached. Written for teaching; the failure modes are from this repository.

## The prompt, as it would be given

> *"Here is a paper claiming a 4-point improvement in retrieval quality from a new chunking method.
> The authors report it on three benchmarks. **Design the experiment that would show they are
> wrong.**"*

## What this shape is testing

Not whether you can critique a paper. **Whether you distinguish a result from a claim**, and
whether you know which parts of a result generalise.

1. Do you attack the **precondition** or the **execution**? Junior critiques find methodology
   errors. Senior critiques find the corpus property the result depends on.
2. Do you know that **absolute numbers and directional findings falsify differently**?
3. Can you say what would make you **accept** it? A critique that cannot be satisfied is not one.

## The 45 minutes

| Minutes | What happens |
|---|---|
| 0–5 | Clarifying. What does "wrong" mean — the number, the direction, or the mechanism? |
| 5–20 | Your experiment |
| 20–35 | Pressure on your **control condition**. This is where it is decided |
| 35–42 | "What result would make you believe them?" |
| 42–45 | Your questions |

## The trap

Most candidates design a **replication** — run the method on a new corpus, see whether 4 points
appears. Necessary, and not falsification: a null result is ambiguous between *the method does not
work* and *this corpus does not have the failure the method fixes*.

The experiment that falsifies **isolates the mechanism**. If the claim is that better chunk
boundaries improve retrieval, a corpus whose boundaries are already good must show **no**
improvement. If it shows 4 points anyway, the stated mechanism is wrong.

comments.body:
Marking this as the answer — the model response, then the rubric.

---

**A strong answer, roughly as I would give it:**

> "First — what would 'wrong' mean here? The number, the direction, or the mechanism? Those need
> different experiments and only the third is interesting.
>
> Assume the mechanism. Their claim is that better chunk boundaries improve retrieval, which
> implies a **precondition**: their corpus had bad boundaries. So the falsifying experiment is a
> corpus where boundaries are already good — structurally chunked documents carrying their heading
> path, each chunk readable in isolation.
>
> If their method still shows 4 points there, it is not doing what they say. It may be doing
> something valuable, but the stated mechanism is wrong, and every adoption decision made on that
> mechanism is unjustified.
>
> **My control matters more than my treatment.** I have to *measure* that my corpus has good
> boundaries rather than assert it — sample twenty chunks, read them cold, check whether you can
> tell what each is about. Ten minutes, and without it my null result is uninterpretable.
>
> I would also run their method on a corpus deliberately given bad boundaries. If it shows a
> **larger** gain there, that is strong positive evidence for their mechanism, and I would rather
> find that than not.
>
> What would make me believe them: a gain that scales with a measured badness-of-boundaries
> statistic across several corpora. That is a much stronger claim than three benchmarks, and it is
> the paper I wish they had written."

---

## Why this scores

| Signal | Weak | Strong |
|---|---|---|
| **Framing** | Designs a replication | Asks what "wrong" means, attacks the mechanism |
| **Control** | Treatment only | Names the control **and how to verify it** |
| **Symmetry** | Only looks for the null | Also designs the arm that would *confirm* them |
| **Falsifiability** | Cannot say what would convince them | Names the result that would |
| **Humility** | "The paper is flawed" | "The claim is broader than the evidence" |

## We ran this on ourselves

[#37](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/discussions/37) measured contextual chunking on this corpus: **worse on both quality
metrics at 2.4× storage.** The reason is exactly the precondition above — structural chunking
already carried the heading path, so these chunks were never orphaned.

**That is not a refutation of contextual chunking.** It demonstrates the technique fixes a failure
we did not have, which is more useful and is what
[The Precondition Test](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/blob/main/docs/60-cheatsheets/frameworks/precondition-test.md) is built
from.
